title: Soil Shake: Parent Guide
endLine: Soil is a mix: big bits sink first, tiny bits last.

scenes.tts: Is dirt just dirt? This cloudy jar holds soil and water. After a shake and a day or two of settling, the soil forms layers.
scenes.caption: Is dirt just dirt? This cloudy jar holds soil and water. After a shake and a day or two of settling, the soil forms layers.
scenes.visual: Friendly schematic kitchen table with a towel. A large clear plastic jar fills about 65 percent of the frame height, swirling with brown muddy water; specks tumble slowly. Big high-contrast question text above: 'Is dirt just dirt?' Then a soft time-lapse shimmer hints at bands forming at the bottom. No photos of real children.
scenes.narration: Is dirt just dirt? This cloudy jar holds soil and water. After a shake and a day or two of settling, the soil forms layers.

scenes.visual: Same jar on the same towel, swirl calming. Title 'Soil Shake' appears to the left of the jar for two seconds.

scenes.tts: It takes about twenty minutes, plus a few quick looks later. Your child practices looking closely, making a guess, and checking it. They also practice waiting for a slow result. And they find out that soil is a mix.
scenes.caption: It takes about twenty minutes, plus a few quick looks later. Your child practices looking closely, making a guess, and checking it. They also practice waiting for a slow result. And they find out that soil is a mix.
scenes.visual: The jar stays at center-right. Three short labels appear one by one beside it, each with a small icon: 'Look closely' (magnifying glass), 'Guess, then check' (pencil and drawing), 'Wait for it' (clock). Specks keep drifting slowly in the water.
scenes.narration: It takes about twenty minutes, plus a few quick looks later. Your child practices looking closely, making a guess, and checking it. They also practice waiting for a slow result. And they find out that soil is a mix.

scenes.tts: You need a clear plastic jar with a lid that screws on tight. Never use glass. Bring about one to one and a half cups of bagged topsoil. Add water, masking tape, a marker, and a ruler.
scenes.caption: You need a clear plastic jar with a lid that screws on tight. Never use glass. Bring about one to one and a half cups of bagged topsoil. Add water, masking tape, a marker, and a ruler.
scenes.visual: The jar is now empty and clean on the towel. Materials slide in and settle in a neat row beside it: a bag of topsoil with a measuring cup, a water pitcher, a roll of masking tape, a marker, a ruler. A glass jar fades in at the edge, gets a red X, and fades out. Label: 'Plastic, never glass'.
scenes.narration: You need a clear plastic jar with a lid that screws on tight. Never use glass. Bring about one to one and a half cups of bagged topsoil. Add water, masking tape, a marker, and a ruler.

scenes.tts: Stay with your child while the soil and water are out. Spread a spoonful of soil on white paper. Look for rock, roots, and leaves together. Ask, 'Does it feel gritty, smooth, or sticky?'
scenes.caption: Stay with your child while the soil and water are out. Spread a spoonful of soil on white paper. Look for rock, roots, and leaves together. Ask, 'Does it feel gritty, smooth, or sticky?'
scenes.visual: A sheet of white paper beside the jar with a small heap of soil. A spoon gently spreads it; zoomed circles highlight a pebble, a thread of root and a brown leaf fleck. Two schematic fingertips rub a pinch of soil; three word chips appear: 'Gritty', 'Smooth', 'Sticky'.
scenes.narration: Stay with your child while the soil and water are out. Spread a spoonful of soil on white paper. Look for rock, roots, and leaves together. Ask, 'Does it feel gritty, smooth, or sticky?'

scenes.tts: Before any water goes in, ask, 'If we shake soil in water and wait, what will it look like?' Have your child draw a guess. Keep it to check later.
scenes.caption: Before any water goes in, ask, 'If we shake soil in water and wait, what will it look like?' Have your child draw a guess. Keep it to check later.
scenes.visual: A speech bubble near the paper: 'What will it look like?' A simple crayon drawing of a jar appears on a second sheet and slides into a folder at the lower left, where it stays for the rest of the film.
scenes.narration: Before any water goes in, ask, 'If we shake soil in water and wait, what will it look like?' Have your child draw a guess. Keep it to check later.

scenes.tts: Pick out sticks and stones bigger than a pea. Fill the jar about one third full of soil. Slowly add water to about one inch from the top. Watch for bubbles. That is air that was in the spaces in the soil.
scenes.caption: Pick out sticks and stones bigger than a pea. Fill the jar about one third full of soil. Slowly add water to about one inch from the top. Watch for bubbles. That is air that was in the spaces in the soil.
scenes.visual: Soil pours into the same jar to a dashed line marked 'one-third'. Water pours in slowly to a second dashed line near the top labeled '1 inch from top'. Small bubbles rise from the soil; one bubble is circled with the label 'air from the soil'.
scenes.narration: Pick out sticks and stones bigger than a pea. Fill the jar about one third full of soil. Slowly add water to about one inch from the top. Watch for bubbles. That is air that was in the spaces in the soil.

scenes.tts: Tighten and check the lid. Take turns shaking hard over a towel for two to three minutes. Have your child sit or stand over the towel and grip with both hands. For ages five to seven, you do the long shaking. Set the jar on a low, steady surface.
scenes.caption: Tighten and check the lid. Take turns shaking hard over a towel for two to three minutes. Have your child sit or stand over the towel and grip with both hands. For ages five to seven, you do the long shaking. Set the jar on a low, steady surface.
scenes.visual: An adult tightens and checks the lid, then shakes the closed jar over the towel. The seated child takes a brief turn using both hands. A timer reads '2 to 3 min'. The adult sets the jar on a low, steady surface.
scenes.narration: Tighten and check the lid. Take turns shaking hard over a towel for two to three minutes. Have your child sit or stand over the towel and grip with both hands. For ages five to seven, you do the long shaking. Set the jar on a low, steady surface.

scenes.tts: Here is a question for you. Inside that cloudy jar are big grains of sand, finer silt, and tiny bits of clay. Which do you think settles first? Which takes the longest?
scenes.caption: Here is a question for you. Inside that cloudy jar are big grains of sand, finer silt, and tiny bits of clay. Which do you think settles first? Which takes the longest?
scenes.visual: The cloudy jar fills the right side. On the left, a high-contrast question card: 'Which settles first? Which takes longest?' Three small chips below it, unsorted: 'sand', 'silt', 'clay', drawn as big, medium and tiny dots.
scenes.narration: Here is a question for you. Inside that cloudy jar are big grains of sand, finer silt, and tiny bits of clay. Which do you think settles first? Which takes the longest?

scenes.visual: Hold the question card and the cloudy jar. Specks drift slowly in the water; a soft ring turns beneath the question. No answer is shown.

scenes.tts: The big bits sink first. After about one minute, sand forms the bottom layer. Your child marks its top with a strip of tape. Dark bits floating on the water are usually old plant parts on their way to becoming humus.
scenes.caption: The big bits sink first. After about one minute, sand forms the bottom layer. Your child marks its top with a strip of tape. Dark bits floating on the water are usually old plant parts on their way to becoming humus.
scenes.visual: Big dots fall fast and pile into a gritty bottom band labeled 'sand'. A strip of tape slides onto the jar's side at the top of that band. Dark flecks rise and float on the surface, labeled 'old plant bits'. A small clock reads '1 minute'.
scenes.narration: The big bits sink first. After about one minute, sand forms the bottom layer. Your child marks its top with a strip of tape. Dark bits floating on the water are usually old plant parts on their way to becoming humus.

scenes.tts: After one hour, look for silt above the sand and mark it with tape. After one to two days, look for clay above it. Measure any layers you can see in centimeters. Clay-rich soil can stay cloudy for days.
scenes.caption: After one hour, look for silt above the sand and mark it with tape. After one to two days, look for clay above it. Measure any layers you can see in centimeters. Clay-rich soil can stay cloudy for days.
scenes.visual: Label the timeline 'Example'. At '1 hour', show silt above sand in this sample and mark it with tape. At '1 to 2 days', show a clay band in this sample and bring a ruler alongside the jar. Add 'Layers can vary'.
scenes.narration: After one hour, look for silt above the sand and mark it with tape. After one to two days, look for clay above it. Measure any layers you can see in centimeters. Clay-rich soil can stay cloudy for days.

scenes.tts: Set the first drawing beside the jar. Ask, 'What matched your guess?' Use the layers to talk about which bits sank first and what is still floating.
scenes.caption: Set the first drawing beside the jar. Ask, 'What matched your guess?' Use the layers to talk about which bits sank first and what is still floating.
scenes.visual: The crayon drawing slides out beside the layered jar. One speech bubble reads 'What matched your guess?' The bottom sand band and the floating plant flecks brighten in turn.
scenes.narration: Set the first drawing beside the jar. Ask, 'What matched your guess?' Use the layers to talk about which bits sank first and what is still floating.

scenes.tts: Small stones can choke children under four, so keep them from babies and toddlers. If a child is choking, call nine one one. Nobody puts soil or muddy fingers in a mouth. Wash hands with soap afterward.
scenes.caption: Small stones can choke children under four, so keep them from babies and toddlers. If a child is choking, call nine one one. Nobody puts soil or muddy fingers in a mouth. Wash hands with soap afterward.
scenes.visual: The layered jar stays at right. Safety badges appear beside it, at most four: an adult and child standing together, a crossed-out pebble labeled 'Under 4: choking risk, call 911', a crossed-out mouth with a muddy finger, and soapy hands under a tap.
scenes.narration: Small stones can choke children under four, so keep them from babies and toddlers. If a child is choking, call nine one one. Nobody puts soil or muddy fingers in a mouth. Wash hands with soap afterward.

scenes.tts: Bagged topsoil is the safest choice. If you plan to dig in a garden, read the guide's soil safety notes before choosing a spot.
scenes.caption: Bagged topsoil is the safest choice. If you plan to dig in a garden, read the guide's soil safety notes before choosing a spot.
scenes.visual: Show a bag of topsoil beside the jar with a green check and the label 'Safest choice'. Show a simple garden bed inset labeled 'Check before digging'.
scenes.narration: Bagged topsoil is the safest choice. If you plan to dig in a garden, read the guide's soil safety notes before choosing a spot.

scenes.tts: That brown stuff on your shoes is a mix. Your child saw the bigger grains settle first and the smaller bits take longer.
scenes.caption: That brown stuff on your shoes is a mix. Your child saw the bigger grains settle first and the smaller bits take longer.
scenes.visual: The finished jar glows softly: sand, silt and clay bands with dark flecks on top, tape marks beside each band. A gentle light shimmer moves down the layers from top to bottom.
scenes.narration: That brown stuff on your shoes is a mix. Your child saw the bigger grains settle first and the smaller bits take longer.

scenes.line: Soil is a mix: big bits sink first, tiny bits last.
scenes.visual: End card with the layered jar faint in the background. Centered, large, high-contrast text: 'Soil is a mix: big bits sink first, tiny bits last.'
